target: Election Day as a national holiday would remove many work/school scheduling barriers and make it easier for eligible voters to cast ballots.
objection: A federal holiday does not automatically give private-sector workers paid time off, so it would not by itself guarantee that most workers can actually use the day to vote.

target: Election Day as a national holiday would be especially helpful for low-income workers because it removes work-schedule barriers.
objection: Low-income workers are concentrated in retail and service jobs where employers are less likely to provide paid time off on federal holidays, so the holiday would often fail to remove their voting barriers.

target: Having Election Day as a holiday would meaningfully increase voter turnout.
objection: Research indicates that an election holiday by itself is not an effective way to increase turnout compared with other voting-access reforms.

target: Election Day should be a national holiday rather than focusing on other reforms.
objection: State-level time-off-for-voting requirements and automatic voter registration are more reliable ways to improve voting access than creating a holiday.

target: A federal holiday does not guarantee paid time off, so it fails to solve the voting problem.
objection: What blocks voting is the lack of available time, not just whether lost time is paid; a holiday can still help by making time available even without a universal paid-leave mandate.

target: Other reforms are a reason to reject the holiday because they are more effective.
objection: Time-off-for-voting and automatic registration address additional barriers, so they can complement a holiday rather than making the holiday inappropriate or ineffective.

target: A holiday would not matter because it would not guarantee paid leave.
objection: Even without paid-leave guarantees, a national holiday would treat voting as a celebration rather than a chore, which can increase civic engagement and participation through motivation rather than compensation.

target: The holiday is not persuasive because paid leave is not guaranteed.
objection: A holiday could still reduce information and friction barriers by enabling schools, election officials, and community organizations to coordinate voter education, reminders, and registration help around a single civic day.

target: The holiday is inferior to other reforms because it does not solve work-time barriers directly.
objection: Polling-place capacity also matters; a holiday can increase poll-worker availability, which may allow more locations or longer hours and thus improve practical access to voting.

target: Low-income workers would still face work-related barriers because employers may not give paid leave on a federal holiday.
objection: Voters are not limited to Election Day daytime voting; early voting and absentee/mail voting reduce the force of the claim that lack of paid leave on the day itself fully determines whether they can vote.

target: A holiday should be rejected because better reforms should be prioritized instead.
objection: A national holiday can be adopted alongside other voting-access reforms, so it is not a reason to reject the holiday as a policy option.

target: Registration reforms can replace a holiday because they are the real fix for voting access.
objection: Automatic registration and similar reforms mainly reduce administrative friction; they do not solve the separate problem of whether voters have time off to cast a ballot on Election Day.

target: Time-off-for-voting reforms are a better substitute than a national holiday.
objection: Time-off-for-voting laws depend on employer compliance and on state-by-state adoption and enforcement, so they are unlikely to eliminate scheduling barriers uniformly nationwide.

target: School/work schedule barriers are the key obstacle, so a holiday is justified.
objection: School-related schedules also matter: parents and guardians can be blocked from voting by weekday school and daycare routines, so a holiday would help by reducing those caregiving constraints too.

target: A federal Election Day holiday would not crowd out or delay other voting-access reforms.
objection: Because policy attention and legislative bandwidth are limited, a high-profile federal holiday could crowd out or slow more targeted reforms like state time-off requirements and automatic voter registration.

target: A federal holiday would reduce or delay more targeted state reforms.
objection: States can still enact their own voting-access laws regardless of a federal holiday, and broad cross-party support for the holiday makes it unlikely to crowd out follow-on reforms.

target: A federal holiday would not reduce or delay state reforms.
objection: Once a visible national holiday is enacted, political urgency for additional reforms usually falls, making it more likely that targeted state reforms will be delayed or weakened.

target: Broad support for the holiday means additional state reforms will also proceed.
objection: Holiday support does not imply the same level of support for more regulatory reforms like employer time-off mandates or automatic voter registration, so those harder reforms may lose momentum.

target: A federal holiday would delay state reforms because it is a substitute for them.
objection: A federal holiday does not legally prevent states from enacting their own voting-access laws, and broad public support makes it likely to keep attention on further reforms rather than substituting for them.

target: A national holiday would remove many work and school scheduling barriers for eligible voters.
objection: A federal holiday does not reliably force employers, schools, or child-care arrangements to close or to provide usable voting time, so it would not reliably remove those barriers.

target: A federal holiday would still meaningfully help low-income workers.
objection: Low-income hourly workers often cannot afford lost wages, and a federal holiday does not guarantee paid time off, so the holiday does not solve their practical barrier to voting.

target: The civic-salience benefits of a holiday can complement other reforms.
objection: Even if civic salience rises, it does not directly overcome the wage-based barrier faced by many low-income workers or reliably translate into turnout gains.

target: A holiday would not delay additional reforms because states can still act.
objection: Employers can argue that a holiday makes new time-off mandates redundant, which increases resistance and can slow or stall state reforms even if the holiday does not legally block them.

target: A federal holiday would produce meaningful turnout gains and support later reforms.
objection: If the holiday produces only limited turnout improvement, it can reduce incentives for policymakers to pursue additional targeted reforms that depend on visible prior gains.

target: A federal holiday would still not meaningfully solve work/school barriers or could delay other reforms.
objection: Because many schools and workplaces close or reduce schedules on national holidays, the holiday would reduce schedule-enforced unavailability and thereby create real voting-access benefits while still allowing states to enact additional reforms.
